meta.topic: 多元微积分：三重积分、曲线积分、格林公式、高斯公式、斯托克斯公式、雅可比行列式

zh: 设 $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ 是有界闭区域，$f$ 在 $\Omega$ 上有界。把 $\Omega$ 分成 $n$ 个小块 $\Delta v_1,\dots,\Delta v_n$（$\Delta v_i$ 兼表体积），在第 $i$ 块任取 $(\xi_i,\eta_i,\zeta_i)$，作黎曼和 $\sum_{i=1}^n f(\xi_i,\eta_i,\zeta_i)\Delta v_i$。若当各小块直径的最大值 $\lambda\to0$ 时，该和趋于与分法、取点都无关的常数 $I$，则 $f$ 在 $\Omega$ 上可积，$I=\iiint_\Omega f\,dV$。有界闭区域上的连续函数一定可积，这是后面所有化归的前提。

若 $\Omega=\{(x,y,z):(x,y)\in D,\ z_1(x,y)\le z\le z_2(x,y)\}$，其中 $D$ 是 $xy$ 平面上的有界闭区域，$z_1,z_2$ 在 $D$ 上连续且 $z_1\le z_2$，并设 $f$ 在 $\Omega$ 上连续。固定 $(x,y)$ 后，$f(x,y,\cdot)$ 在区间 $[z_1(x,y),z_2(x,y)]$ 上连续，故 $F(x,y)=\int_{z_1(x,y)}^{z_2(x,y)}f(x,y,z)\,dz$ 存在且连续。按 $xy$ 平面上的小矩形分块，把沿每条竖线的黎曼和换成关于 $z$ 的积分，再令分块直径趋于零，由二重积分的定义得 $$\iiint_\Omega f\,dV=\iint_D\left[\int_{z_1(x,y)}^{z_2(x,y)}f(x,y,z)\,dz\right]dx\,dy.$$ 截面法 $\int_a^b\left[\iint_{D_z}f\,dx\,dy\right]dz$ 是同一 Fubini 结论的另一种累次次序，它要求每个水平截面 $D_z$ 可积。

设 $T:\Omega'\to\Omega$，$(u,v,w)\mapsto(x,y,z)$，$x,y,z$ 有连续偏导数，$T$ 在 $\Omega'$ 内部一一对应，且雅可比行列式 $$J=\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}=\begin{vmatrix}x_u&x_v&x_w\\ y_u&y_v&y_w\\ z_u&z_v&z_w\end{vmatrix}$$ 在内部除一个体积为零的集合外不为零。把 $\Omega'$ 分成边长 $\Delta u,\Delta v,\Delta w$ 的小长方体，$T$ 在一点附近由微分线性化：小长方体被映成以 $T_u\Delta u,T_v\Delta v,T_w\Delta w$ 为棱的平行六面体，其体积为 $|J|\Delta u\Delta v\Delta w$。于是 $\Omega$ 中小块的体积 $\Delta V\approx|J|\Delta u\Delta v\Delta w$，代入黎曼和并令网格直径趋于零，得 $$\iiint_\Omega f\,dV=\iiint_{\Omega'}f(T(u,v,w))\,|J|\,du\,dv\,dw.$$ 条件 $J\ne0$（除零测集外）由反函数定理保证 $T$ 局部可逆，避免把区域折叠计算两次。

柱坐标 $x=r\cos\theta,\ y=r\sin\theta,\ z=z$，其中 $r\ge0,\ 0\le\theta<2\pi$。偏导数矩阵为 $$\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-r\sin\theta&0\\ \sin\theta&r\cos\theta&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},$$ 沿第一行展开得 $J=\cos\theta\cdot r\cos\theta-(-r\sin\theta)\sin\theta=r(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)=r$。在 $r\ge0$ 上 $|J|=r$，故 $$dV=r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz.$$ 因子 $r$ 不能漏：它正是极坐标面积元 $r\,dr\,d\theta$ 在三维中的延续。区域或被积函数含 $x^2+y^2$、具有绕 $z$ 轴旋转对称性时，柱坐标最合适。

球坐标 $x=\rho\sin\varphi\cos\theta,\ y=\rho\sin\varphi\sin\theta,\ z=\rho\cos\varphi$，其中 $\rho\ge0,\ 0\le\varphi\le\pi,\ 0\le\theta<2\pi$。直接展开雅可比行列式得 $$J=\rho^2\sin\varphi.$$ 在 $0\le\varphi\le\pi$ 上 $\sin\varphi\ge0$，故 $|J|=\rho^2\sin\varphi$，$$dV=\rho^2\sin\varphi\,d\rho\,d\varphi\,d\theta.$$ 当 $\rho=0$ 或 $\varphi=0,\pi$ 时 $J=0$，但这些点集体积为零，不影响积分；在内部 $\rho>0,\ 0<\varphi<\pi$ 上变换是一一的。

例：单位球 $B=\{\rho\le1\}$ 的体积。取 $f\equiv1$，则 $$\begin{aligned}V&=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\int_0^1 \rho^2\sin\varphi\,d\rho\,d\varphi\,d\theta\\&=\frac{1}{3}\cdot2\cdot2\pi=\frac{4\pi}{3}.\end{aligned}$$ 这里对 $\rho$ 积分得 $1/3$，对 $\varphi$ 积分得 $2$，对 $\theta$ 积分得 $2\pi$。注意：换元公式中的 $|J|$ 必须取绝对值；若变换只在内部一一对应、在边界上重叠（如 $\theta=0$ 与 $\theta=2\pi$ 表示同一半平面），边界是零测集，不影响积分值，但不能因此把内部也当成多对一。
en: Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded closed region and let $f$ be bounded on $\Omega$. Partition $\Omega$ into $n$ pieces $\Delta v_1,\dots,\Delta v_n$ ($\Delta v_i$ also denoting volume), choose $(\xi_i,\eta_i,\zeta_i)$ in the $i$-th piece, and form the Riemann sum $\sum_{i=1}^n f(\xi_i,\eta_i,\zeta_i)\Delta v_i$. If, as the largest diameter $\lambda\to0$, this sum tends to a constant $I$ independent of the partition and the sample points, then $f$ is integrable on $\Omega$ and $I=\iiint_\Omega f\,dV$. Every continuous function on a bounded closed region is integrable; this is the hypothesis underlying all the reductions below.

Suppose $\Omega=\{(x,y,z):(x,y)\in D,\ z_1(x,y)\le z\le z_2(x,y)\}$, where $D$ is a bounded closed region in the $xy$-plane, $z_1,z_2$ are continuous on $D$ with $z_1\le z_2$, and $f$ is continuous on $\Omega$. For fixed $(x,y)$, the function $f(x,y,\cdot)$ is continuous on $[z_1(x,y),z_2(x,y)]$, so $F(x,y)=\int_{z_1(x,y)}^{z_2(x,y)}f(x,y,z)\,dz$ exists and is continuous. Partitioning according to small rectangles in the $xy$-plane, replacing the Riemann sum along each vertical line by the $z$-integral, and letting the mesh tend to zero, the definition of the double integral gives $$\iiint_\Omega f\,dV=\iint_D\left[\int_{z_1(x,y)}^{z_2(x,y)}f(x,y,z)\,dz\right]dx\,dy.$$ The slicing formula $\int_a^b\left[\iint_{D_z}f\,dx\,dy\right]dz$ is the same Fubini statement with the iterated order reversed; it requires each horizontal section $D_z$ to be integrable.

Let $T:\Omega'\to\Omega$, $(u,v,w)\mapsto(x,y,z)$, have continuous partial derivatives, be one-to-one on the interior of $\Omega'$, and have Jacobian $$J=\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}=\begin{vmatrix}x_u&x_v&x_w\\ y_u&y_v&y_w\\ z_u&z_v&z_w\end{vmatrix}$$ nonzero on the interior except on a set of volume zero. Partition $\Omega'$ into small boxes of side lengths $\Delta u,\Delta v,\Delta w$. Near a point, $T$ is linearized by its differential: a small box is mapped to the parallelepiped with edge vectors $T_u\Delta u,T_v\Delta v,T_w\Delta w$, whose volume is $|J|\Delta u\Delta v\Delta w$. Hence a small piece of $\Omega$ has volume $\Delta V\approx|J|\Delta u\Delta v\Delta w$. Substituting into the Riemann sum and letting the mesh tend to zero yields $$\iiint_\Omega f\,dV=\iiint_{\Omega'}f(T(u,v,w))\,|J|\,du\,dv\,dw.$$ The condition $J\ne0$ off a null set ensures, via the inverse function theorem, that $T$ is locally invertible and prevents folding, which would count some points twice.

In cylindrical coordinates $x=r\cos\theta,\ y=r\sin\theta,\ z=z$, where $r\ge0,\ 0\le\theta<2\pi$, the matrix of partial derivatives is $$\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-r\sin\theta&0\\ \sin\theta&r\cos\theta&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$ Expanding along the first row gives $J=\cos\theta\cdot r\cos\theta-(-r\sin\theta)\sin\theta=r(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)=r$. Since $r\ge0$, $|J|=r$, hence $$dV=r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz.$$ The factor $r$ must not be omitted: it is the three-dimensional continuation of the polar area element $r\,dr\,d\theta$. These coordinates suit regions or integrands involving $x^2+y^2$ and rotational symmetry about the $z$-axis.

In spherical coordinates $x=\rho\sin\varphi\cos\theta,\ y=\rho\sin\varphi\sin\theta,\ z=\rho\cos\varphi$, where $\rho\ge0,\ 0\le\varphi\le\pi,\ 0\le\theta<2\pi$, a direct expansion of the Jacobian determinant gives $$J=\rho^2\sin\varphi.$$ On $0\le\varphi\le\pi$ we have $\sin\varphi\ge0$, so $|J|=\rho^2\sin\varphi$ and $$dV=\rho^2\sin\varphi\,d\rho\,d\varphi\,d\theta.$$ When $\rho=0$ or $\varphi=0,\pi$, $J=0$, but these sets have volume zero and do not affect the integral; on the interior $\rho>0,\ 0<\varphi<\pi$ the map is one-to-one.

Example: the volume of the unit ball $B=\{\rho\le1\}$. Taking $f\equiv1$, $$\begin{aligned}V&=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\int_0^1 \rho^2\sin\varphi\,d\rho\,d\varphi\,d\theta\\&=\frac{1}{3}\cdot2\cdot2\pi=\frac{4\pi}{3}.\end{aligned}$$ Here the $\rho$-integral gives $1/3$, the $\varphi$-integral gives $2$, and the $\theta$-integral gives $2\pi$. Caution: the factor $|J|$ in the change-of-variables formula is an absolute value. If the map is one-to-one on the interior but identifies boundary pieces (e.g. $\theta=0$ and $\theta=2\pi$ describe the same half-plane), the boundary is a null set and does not affect the value, but the interior must not be multiply covered.

zh: 设 $L$ 是分段光滑曲线弧，$f$ 在 $L$ 上连续。把 $L$ 分成 $n$ 小段，第 $i$ 段弧长为 $\Delta s_i$，在其上任取点 $M_i$，作和 $\sum_{i=1}^n f(M_i)\Delta s_i$；当最大弧长趋于零时，若极限存在且与分法、取点无关，就记为 $\int_L f\,ds$。若 $L$ 由 $r(t)=(x(t),y(t))$，$a\le t\le b$ 给出，$r'$ 连续且 $r'\ne0$，则 $$ds=|r'(t)|\,dt=\sqrt{x'(t)^2+y'(t)^2}\,dt,\qquad \int_L f\,ds=\int_a^b f(r(t))|r'(t)|\,dt.$$ 这里 $ds>0$，下限 $a$ 必须小于上限 $b$：改变曲线方向只把 $t$ 换成 $a+b-t$，$|r'|$ 不变，故第一类曲线积分与定向无关。

第二类曲线积分 $\int_L P\,dx+Q\,dy$ 来自黎曼和 $\sum_{i=1}^n[P(M_i)\Delta x_i+Q(M_i)\Delta y_i]$，其中 $\Delta x_i,\Delta y_i$ 是第 $i$ 段终点减起点的有向增量，可正可负。若 $L$ 由 $r(t)$ 从 $t=\alpha$ 到 $t=\beta$ 描写（$\alpha$ 对应起点、$\beta$ 对应终点，不要求 $\alpha<\beta$），则 $dx=x'(t)\,dt,\ dy=y'(t)\,dt$，$$\int_L P\,dx+Q\,dy=\int_\alpha^\beta\left[P(r(t))x'(t)+Q(r(t))y'(t)\right]dt.$$ 定向已编码在「从 $\alpha$ 积到 $\beta$」中；交换起点与终点，积分上下限随之互换。

设 $L^-$ 是 $L$ 的反向曲线，用 $r^-(t)=r(\alpha+\beta-t)$，$t\in[\alpha,\beta]$ 参数化，则 $(r^-)'(t)=-r'(\alpha+\beta-t)$。于是 $$\int_{L^-}F\cdot dr=\int_\alpha^\beta F(r(\alpha+\beta-t))\cdot\left(-r'(\alpha+\beta-t)\right)dt.$$ 令 $s=\alpha+\beta-t$，则 $dt=-ds$，$t=\alpha$ 对应 $s=\beta$，$t=\beta$ 对应 $s=\alpha$，故上式 $$=\int_\beta^\alpha F(r(s))\cdot r'(s)\,ds=-\int_\alpha^\beta F(r(s))\cdot r'(s)\,ds=-\int_L F\cdot dr.$$ 对第一类积分，$ds=|(r^-)'|dt=|r'|dt$，故 $\int_{L^-}f\,ds=\int_L f\,ds$。结论：第二类变号，第一类不变，这是两类积分最本质的区别。

若曲线在每点有单位切向量 $T=(\cos\alpha,\cos\beta)$，且 $T$ 的方向与 $L$ 的定向一致，则沿曲线走一小段 $ds$ 时 $dx=\cos\alpha\,ds,\ dy=\cos\beta\,ds$。代入得 $$\int_L P\,dx+Q\,dy=\int_L(P\cos\alpha+Q\cos\beta)\,ds.$$ 若 $F=(P,Q)$，右端就是 $\int_L F\cdot T\,ds$，即切向分量沿弧长的积分；第二类曲线积分因此可解释为力 $F$ 沿有向路径所做的功。这里 $T$ 的定向必须与 $L$ 一致，否则 $dx,dy$ 的符号会整体反号。

例：$F=(-y,x)$，$L$ 为单位圆 $x=\cos t,\ y=\sin t$。逆时针取 $t:0\to2\pi$，则 $$\int_L F\cdot dr=\int_0^{2\pi}\left[(-\sin t)(-\sin t)+(\cos t)(\cos t)\right]dt=\int_0^{2\pi}1\,dt=2\pi.$$ 顺时针取 $t:2\pi\to0$（或仍取 $t:0\to2\pi$ 但用 $(\cos(-t),\sin(-t))$），同一计算给出 $-2\pi$。被积函数相同、路径相同，只是定向相反，值就变号；这再次说明第二类曲线积分是有向积分。

若 $F=
abla u$ 在连通开区域 $D$ 上成立，$L\subset D$ 分段光滑，起点为 $A$、终点为 $B$，则沿 $r(t)$ 有 $$ rac{d}{dt}u(r(t))=
abla u(r(t))\cdot r'(t)=F(r(t))\cdot r'(t).$$ 由牛顿–莱布尼茨公式得 $$\int_L F\cdot dr=u(B)-u(A).$$ 因此积分只与端点有关，沿任意闭曲线为零；反过来，若闭路积分全为零，可定义 $u(x)=\int_A^x F\cdot dr$ 并验证 $
abla u=F$。定向的作用仅在于端点次序：交换 $A,B$ 时右端变号。注意这个势函数结论要求 $D$ 连通（通常单连通）且 $F$ 连续；仅「旋度为零」在非单连通区域不足以保证整体势函数存在。
en: Let $L$ be a piecewise smooth arc and let $f$ be continuous on $L$. Subdivide $L$ into $n$ small arcs of lengths $\Delta s_i$, choose a point $M_i$ on the $i$-th arc, and form the sum $\sum_{i=1}^n f(M_i)\Delta s_i$. If the limit as the largest arc length tends to zero exists independently of the subdivision and the sample points, it is denoted $\int_L f\,ds$. If $L$ is given by $r(t)=(x(t),y(t))$, $a\le t\le b$, with $r'$ continuous and nonzero, then $$ds=|r'(t)|\,dt=\sqrt{x'(t)^2+y'(t)^2}\,dt,\qquad \int_L f\,ds=\int_a^b f(r(t))|r'(t)|\,dt.$$ Here $ds>0$ and the lower limit $a$ must be smaller than $b$: reversing the curve only replaces $t$ by $a+b-t$, which leaves $|r'|$ unchanged, so a first-kind line integral is independent of orientation.

The second-kind line integral $\int_L P\,dx+Q\,dy$ comes from the Riemann sum $\sum_{i=1}^n[P(M_i)\Delta x_i+Q(M_i)\Delta y_i]$, where $\Delta x_i,\Delta y_i$ are the signed increments from the initial to the terminal point of the $i$-th piece and may be positive or negative. If $L$ is described by $r(t)$ from $t=\alpha$ to $t=\beta$ ($\alpha$ the starting parameter and $\beta$ the ending parameter, not necessarily $\alpha<\beta$), then $dx=x'(t)\,dt,\ dy=y'(t)\,dt$, and $$\int_L P\,dx+Q\,dy=\int_\alpha^\beta\left[P(r(t))x'(t)+Q(r(t))y'(t)\right]dt.$$ The orientation is encoded in integrating from $\alpha$ to $\beta$; interchanging the endpoints interchanges the limits.

Let $L^-$ be the reversed curve, parametrized by $r^-(t)=r(\alpha+\beta-t)$, $t\in[\alpha,\beta]$. Then $(r^-)'(t)=-r'(\alpha+\beta-t)$, so $$\int_{L^-}F\cdot dr=\int_\alpha^\beta F(r(\alpha+\beta-t))\cdot\left(-r'(\alpha+\beta-t)\right)dt.$$ Put $s=\alpha+\beta-t$; then $dt=-ds$, $t=\alpha$ corresponds to $s=\beta$, and $t=\beta$ to $s=\alpha$, hence the last integral equals $$\int_\beta^\alpha F(r(s))\cdot r'(s)\,ds=-\int_\alpha^\beta F(r(s))\cdot r'(s)\,ds=-\int_L F\cdot dr.$$ For a first-kind integral, $ds=|(r^-)'|dt=|r'|dt$, so $\int_{L^-}f\,ds=\int_L f\,ds$. Conclusion: the second kind changes sign, the first kind does not; this is the essential difference between the two.

If the curve has a unit tangent vector $T=(\cos\alpha,\cos\beta)$ whose direction agrees with the orientation of $L$, then moving a distance $ds$ along the curve gives $dx=\cos\alpha\,ds,\ dy=\cos\beta\,ds$. Substitution yields $$\int_L P\,dx+Q\,dy=\int_L(P\cos\alpha+Q\cos\beta)\,ds.$$ For $F=(P,Q)$ the right side is $\int_L F\cdot T\,ds$, the integral of the tangential component with respect to arc length; this is why the second-kind integral represents the work done by $F$ along the oriented path. The direction of $T$ must match the orientation of $L$; otherwise the signs of $dx$ and $dy$ are globally reversed.

Example: $F=(-y,x)$ and $L$ the unit circle $x=\cos t,\ y=\sin t$. Traversed counterclockwise with $t:0\to2\pi$, $$\int_L F\cdot dr=\int_0^{2\pi}\left[(-\sin t)(-\sin t)+(\cos t)(\cos t)\right]dt=\int_0^{2\pi}1\,dt=2\pi.$$ Clockwise, with $t:2\pi\to0$ (or still $t:0\to2\pi$ but using $(\cos(-t),\sin(-t))$), the same computation gives $-2\pi$. The integrand and the path are the same; only the orientation is reversed, and the value changes sign. This again shows that a second-kind line integral is an oriented integral.

If $F=
abla u$ on a connected open region $D$ and $L\subset D$ is piecewise smooth with initial point $A$ and terminal point $B$, then along $r(t)$, $$ rac{d}{dt}u(r(t))=
abla u(r(t))\cdot r'(t)=F(r(t))\cdot r'(t).$$ By the fundamental theorem of calculus, $$\int_L F\cdot dr=u(B)-u(A).$$ Hence the integral depends only on the endpoints and vanishes on every closed curve; conversely, if all closed-loop integrals vanish, one defines $u(x)=\int_A^x F\cdot dr$ and checks that $
abla u=F$. Orientation enters only through the order of the endpoints: interchanging $A$ and $B$ changes the sign of the right side. This potential conclusion requires $D$ to be connected (usually simply connected) and $F$ continuous; vanishing curl alone is insufficient on a non-simply-connected region.

zh: 设 $D$ 是由分段光滑闭曲线 $L$ 围成的有界闭区域，$L$ 取正向：沿 $L$ 前进时 $D$ 始终在左手边（外边界为逆时针）。设 $P,Q$ 在包含 $D$ 的开集上有连续一阶偏导数，则 $$\oint_L P\,dx+Q\,dy=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)dx\,dy.$$ 左端是环流，右端是旋度 $z$ 分量的面积分。三个条件——$L$ 封闭且分段光滑、$L$ 取正向、$P,Q$ 在 $D$ 上 $C^1$——缺一不可；特别地，若 $D$ 内有使偏导数不存在的奇点，不能直接套用。

先设 $D$ 是 $x$ 型区域：$$D=\{(x,y):a\le x\le b,\ \varphi_1(x)\le y\le\varphi_2(x)\},$$ 其中 $\varphi_1,\varphi_2$ 连续。对 $P$ 用牛顿–莱布尼茨公式：$$\iint_D\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\,dx\,dy=\int_a^b\left[P(x,\varphi_2(x))-P(x,\varphi_1(x))\right]dx.$$ 正向边界由下边 $y=\varphi_1$（左到右）、右边、上边 $y=\varphi_2$（右到左）、左边组成；竖直边上 $dx=0$，对 $\oint P\,dx$ 无贡献，故 $$\begin{aligned}\oint_L P\,dx&=\int_a^b P(x,\varphi_1(x))dx+\int_b^a P(x,\varphi_2(x))dx\\&=-\int_a^b\left[P(x,\varphi_2)-P(x,\varphi_1)\right]dx.\end{aligned}$$ 比较两式得 $\oint_L P\,dx=-\iint_D P_y\,dxdy$。

同理，若 $D$ 也是 $y$ 型区域 $c\le y\le d,\ \psi_1(y)\le x\le\psi_2(y)$，对 $Q$ 用牛顿–莱布尼茨公式，并注意水平边上 $dy=0$，得 $$\oint_L Q\,dy=\iint_D\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}\,dx\,dy.$$ 若 $D$ 同时是 $x$ 型与 $y$ 型区域，两式相加即得格林公式。一般的有界区域可用有限条光滑曲线分成有限个同时为两型的子区域；在公共内边界上，两个相邻子区域诱导的方向相反，线积分沿公共边两两抵消，只剩外边界 $L$，而二重积分对子区域可加。故公式对有限个两型区域之并成立。

定向的作用：若把 $L$ 反向记为 $L^-$，则 $\oint_{L^-}=-\oint_L$，而右端的二重积分不变，所以使用反向边界时必须写成 $$\oint_{L^-}P\,dx+Q\,dy=-\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)dx\,dy.$$ 对多连通区域（带洞），把每条边界都按「区域在左侧」定向：外边界逆时针、内边界顺时针，并对所有边界求和，公式仍为 $$\sum_j\oint_{L_j}P\,dx+Q\,dy=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)dx\,dy.$$ 内边界反向不是随意约定，而是保证区域始终在左侧，使公式对每个边界分量一致成立。

若 $D$ 单连通（区域内任一闭曲线可在 $D$ 内连续收缩为一点，等价地 $D$ 没有洞），且 $P_y=Q_x$ 在 $D$ 上处处成立，则对 $D$ 内任一分段光滑的简单闭曲线 $L$，其内部也含于 $D$，由格林公式 $$\begin{aligned}\oint_L P\,dx+Q\,dy&=\iint_{\operatorname{int}L}\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)dx\,dy\\&=0.\end{aligned}$$ 一般闭曲线可分解为有限个简单闭曲线，故沿任意闭曲线的积分都为零，积分与路径无关。单连通不能去掉：在 $D=\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}$ 上取 $$P=-\frac{y}{x^2+y^2},\qquad Q=\frac{x}{x^2+y^2},$$ 直接求导得 $P_y=Q_x=\frac{y^2-x^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}$，但沿单位圆逆时针 $$\oint P\,dx+Q\,dy=\int_0^{2\pi}1\,dt=2\pi\ne0.$$ 原因是单位圆内部包含奇点 $0$，$P,Q$ 在 $L$ 围成的区域内不满足 $C^1$ 条件。

取 $P=-y,\ Q=x$，则 $Q_x-P_y=1-(-1)=2$，格林公式给出 $$A(D)=\iint_D1\,dx\,dy=\frac12\oint_L(x\,dy-y\,dx).$$ 类似地，取 $(P,Q)=(0,x)$ 得 $A=\oint_L x\,dy$，取 $(-y,0)$ 得 $A=-\oint_L y\,dx$。例：椭圆 $x=a\cos t,\ y=b\sin t$，$t:0\to2\pi$，则 $$\frac12\oint_L(x\,dy-y\,dx)=\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}(ab\cos^2t+ab\sin^2t)\,dt=\pi ab.$$ 使用这些面积公式同样要求 $L$ 正向、$P,Q$ 在 $D$ 上 $C^1$；这里取的是多项式，后一条件自动满足。
en: Let $D$ be a bounded closed region bounded by a piecewise smooth closed curve $L$ taken in the positive direction: walking along $L$, the region $D$ stays on the left (the outer boundary is counterclockwise). Let $P,Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open set containing $D$. Then $$\oint_L P\,dx+Q\,dy=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)dx\,dy.$$ The left side is the circulation, the right side the area integral of the $z$-component of the curl. All three hypotheses — $L$ closed and piecewise smooth, $L$ positively oriented, and $P,Q$ of class $C^1$ on $D$ — are needed; in particular, a singular point inside $D$ where the partials fail prevents a direct application.

First suppose $D$ is an $x$-type region: $$D=\{(x,y):a\le x\le b,\ \varphi_1(x)\le y\le\varphi_2(x)\},$$ with $\varphi_1,\varphi_2$ continuous. Apply the fundamental theorem of calculus to $P$: $$\iint_D\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\,dx\,dy=\int_a^b\left[P(x,\varphi_2(x))-P(x,\varphi_1(x))\right]dx.$$ The positively oriented boundary consists of the lower edge $y=\varphi_1$ (left to right), the right side, the upper edge $y=\varphi_2$ (right to left), and the left side; on the vertical sides $dx=0$, so they do not contribute to $\oint P\,dx$. Hence $$\begin{aligned}\oint_L P\,dx&=\int_a^b P(x,\varphi_1(x))dx+\int_b^a P(x,\varphi_2(x))dx\\&=-\int_a^b\left[P(x,\varphi_2)-P(x,\varphi_1)\right]dx.\end{aligned}$$ Comparing the two expressions gives $\oint_L P\,dx=-\iint_D P_y\,dxdy$.

Similarly, if $D$ is also a $y$-type region $c\le y\le d,\ \psi_1(y)\le x\le\psi_2(y)$, applying the fundamental theorem of calculus to $Q$ and noting that $dy=0$ on horizontal edges gives $$\oint_L Q\,dy=\iint_D\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}\,dx\,dy.$$ If $D$ is simultaneously of $x$-type and $y$-type, adding the two identities yields Green's theorem. A general bounded region can be cut by finitely many smooth curves into finitely many subregions each of both types; on a common internal edge the two induced orientations are opposite, so the line integrals cancel in pairs and only the outer boundary $L$ remains, while the double integral is additive over the subregions. Hence the formula holds for finite unions of such regions.

Role of orientation: if $L$ is reversed and denoted $L^-$, then $\oint_{L^-}=-\oint_L$ while the double integral is unchanged, so with the reversed boundary one must write $$\oint_{L^-}P\,dx+Q\,dy=-\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)dx\,dy.$$ For a multiply connected region (with holes), orient every boundary component so that the region stays on the left: the outer boundary counterclockwise and the inner boundaries clockwise, and sum over all components: $$\sum_j\oint_{L_j}P\,dx+Q\,dy=\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)dx\,dy.$$ Reversing the inner boundaries is not an arbitrary convention: it keeps the region on the left and makes the formula consistent on every boundary component.

If $D$ is simply connected (every closed curve in $D$ can be contracted continuously to a point inside $D$; equivalently, $D$ has no holes) and $P_y=Q_x$ holds everywhere in $D$, then for every piecewise smooth simple closed curve $L$ in $D$, its interior is contained in $D$, and Green's theorem gives $$\begin{aligned}\oint_L P\,dx+Q\,dy&=\iint_{\operatorname{int}L}\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)dx\,dy\\&=0.\end{aligned}$$ A general closed curve decomposes into finitely many simple ones, so the integral over every closed curve vanishes and the integral is path-independent. Simple connectivity cannot be dropped: on $D=\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}$ take $$P=-\frac{y}{x^2+y^2},\qquad Q=\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}.$$ Direct differentiation gives $P_y=Q_x=\frac{y^2-x^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}$, yet counterclockwise around the unit circle $$\oint P\,dx+Q\,dy=\int_0^{2\pi}1\,dt=2\pi\ne0.$$ The reason is that the interior of the unit circle contains the singular point $0$, so $P,Q$ fail the $C^1$ hypothesis on the region enclosed by $L$.

Taking $P=-y,\ Q=x$ gives $Q_x-P_y=1-(-1)=2$, so Green's theorem yields $$A(D)=\iint_D1\,dx\,dy=\frac12\oint_L(x\,dy-y\,dx).$$ Similarly, $(P,Q)=(0,x)$ gives $A=\oint_L x\,dy$, and $(-y,0)$ gives $A=-\oint_L y\,dx$. Example: the ellipse $x=a\cos t,\ y=b\sin t$, $t:0\to2\pi$, gives $$\frac12\oint_L(x\,dy-y\,dx)=\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}(ab\cos^2t+ab\sin^2t)\,dt=\pi ab.$$ These area formulas again require $L$ positively oriented and $P,Q$ of class $C^1$ on $D$; for the polynomial fields chosen here the latter condition is automatic.

zh: 设 $\Omega$ 是由分片光滑闭曲面 $\Sigma=\partial\Omega$ 围成的有界闭区域，$\Sigma$ 取外侧，即单位法向量 $n$ 指向 $\Omega$ 外部；设 $F=(P,Q,R)$ 在 $\Omega$ 上有连续一阶偏导数。则 $$\begin{aligned}\oiint_\Sigma F\cdot n\,dS&=\iiint_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dV,\\ \operatorname{div}F&=\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial R}{\partial z}.\end{aligned}$$ 坐标形式为 $$\begin{aligned}\oiint_\Sigma &P\,dy\,dz+Q\,dz\,dx+R\,dx\,dy\\&=\iiint_\Omega(P_x+Q_y+R_z)\,dV.\end{aligned}$$ 条件：曲面封闭、取外侧、$F$ 在 $\Omega$ 上 $C^1$；缺一项都会改变符号或使公式不成立。

先设 $\Omega$ 是 $z$ 型区域：$$\Omega=\{(x,y,z):(x,y)\in D,\ z_1(x,y)\le z\le z_2(x,y)\},$$ 其中 $D$ 有界、$z_1,z_2$ 连续。对固定的 $(x,y)$，由牛顿–莱布尼茨公式 $$\int_{z_1(x,y)}^{z_2(x,y)}\frac{\partial R}{\partial z}\,dz=R(x,y,z_2(x,y))-R(x,y,z_1(x,y)).$$ 两边在 $D$ 上积分得 $$\iiint_\Omega R_z\,dV=\iint_D\left[R(x,y,z_2)-R(x,y,z_1)\right]dxdy.$$ 再看通量：上表面 $z=z_2$ 的外法向 $z$ 分量为正，且 $n_z\,dS=dxdy$；下表面 $z=z_1$ 的外法向 $z$ 分量为负，$n_z\,dS=-dxdy$；侧面法向与 $z$ 轴垂直，$n_z=0$。故 $$\oiint_\Sigma R n_z\,dS=\iint_D R(x,y,z_2)\,dxdy-\iint_D R(x,y,z_1)\,dxdy.$$ 两式相等，即 $\oiint_\Sigma R n_z\,dS=\iiint_\Omega R_z\,dV$。

对 $P$ 分量，若 $\Omega$ 可看成 $x$ 型区域（沿 $x$ 方向穿入、穿出各一次），同样由微积分基本定理得 $$\oiint_\Sigma P n_x\,dS=\iiint_\Omega P_x\,dV;$$ 对 $Q$ 分量，把 $\Omega$ 看成 $y$ 型区域得 $$\oiint_\Sigma Q n_y\,dS=\iiint_\Omega Q_y\,dV.$$ 三式相加，左端为 $\oiint_\Sigma(P n_x+Q n_y+R n_z)\,dS=\oiint_\Sigma F\cdot n\,dS$，右端为 $\iiint_\Omega(P_x+Q_y+R_z)\,dV$，即高斯公式。若 $\Omega$ 不能同时写成三种简单区域，可用有限个分片光滑曲面把它分成有限个这样的子区域；内部公共曲面上两侧的外法向相反，通量相消，三重积分可加，结论仍成立。

定向检验：取 $\Omega$ 为单位球 $x^2+y^2+z^2\le1$，$F=(x,y,z)$。则 $\operatorname{div}F=3$，故 $$\oiint_\Sigma F\cdot n\,dS=\iiint_\Omega3\,dV=3\cdot\frac{4\pi}{3}=4\pi.$$ 直接算：球面外侧单位法向 $n=(x,y,z)$，在球面上 $F\cdot n=x^2+y^2+z^2=1$，故通量为 $\oiint_\Sigma1\,dS=4\pi$，两者一致。若误取内侧，$n$ 变为 $-(x,y,z)$，通量为 $-4\pi$；这正说明「外法向」不是无关紧要的约定。

把 $\Omega$ 收缩到内点 $M$。若 $F$ 在 $M$ 处 $C^1$，则 $\operatorname{div}F$ 在 $M$ 连续；由积分中值定理（或介值性）存在 $M_\Omega\in\Omega$ 使 $$\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{V(\Omega)}&\oiint_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot n\,dS\\&=\frac{1}{V(\Omega)}\iiint_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dV=\operatorname{div}F(M_\Omega).\end{aligned}$$ 当 $\Omega$ 收缩到 $M$ 时 $M_\Omega\to M$，由连续性得 $$\operatorname{div}F(M)=\lim_{\Omega\to M}\frac{1}{V(\Omega)}\oiint_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot n\,dS.$$ 这就是「散度是单位体积的通量」的精确含义：正散度表示源，负散度表示汇。极限要求区域按可控方式收缩、$F$ 在 $M$ 的邻域内 $C^1$。

高斯公式要求 $F$ 在 $\Omega$ 上处处 $C^1$，奇点不能忽略。例如 $F(r)=r/|r|^3$（$r\ne0$）满足 $\operatorname{div}F=0$，但取 $\Sigma$ 为以原点为球心、半径 $\varepsilon$ 的球面并取外侧，直接在球面上算：$n=r/\varepsilon$，$F\cdot n=1/\varepsilon^2$，故 $$\oiint_\Sigma F\cdot n\,dS=\frac{1}{\varepsilon^2}\cdot4\pi\varepsilon^2=4\pi\ne0.$$ 若对区域 $\{\varepsilon\le|r|\le1\}$ 用高斯公式，内部散度为 $0$，而外球面通量为 $4\pi$、内球面通量为 $-4\pi$（对该区域而言内球面的外法向指向原点），合计 $0$，与三重积分一致。这说明：奇点在区域内部时不能把 $\Sigma$ 直接缩成一点，必须挖去小球，再对挖洞后的区域应用公式。
en: Let $\Omega$ be a bounded closed region bounded by a piecewise smooth closed surface $\Sigma=\partial\Omega$ taken on the outer side, i.e. the unit normal $n$ points outside $\Omega$. Let $F=(P,Q,R)$ have continuous first partial derivatives on $\Omega$. Then $$\begin{aligned}\oiint_\Sigma F\cdot n\,dS&=\iiint_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dV,\\ \operatorname{div}F&=\frac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial R}{\partial z}.\end{aligned}$$ In coordinates, $$\begin{aligned}\oiint_\Sigma &P\,dy\,dz+Q\,dz\,dx+R\,dx\,dy\\&=\iiint_\Omega(P_x+Q_y+R_z)\,dV.\end{aligned}$$ Hypotheses: the surface is closed, taken on the outer side, and $F$ is $C^1$ on $\Omega$; omitting any one changes the sign or invalidates the formula.

First suppose $\Omega$ is $z$-simple: $$\Omega=\{(x,y,z):(x,y)\in D,\ z_1(x,y)\le z\le z_2(x,y)\},$$ where $D$ is bounded and $z_1,z_2$ are continuous. For fixed $(x,y)$, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives $$\int_{z_1(x,y)}^{z_2(x,y)}\frac{\partial R}{\partial z}\,dz=R(x,y,z_2(x,y))-R(x,y,z_1(x,y)).$$ Integrating over $D$ yields $$\iiint_\Omega R_z\,dV=\iint_D\left[R(x,y,z_2)-R(x,y,z_1)\right]dxdy.$$ Now consider the flux: on the upper surface $z=z_2$ the outward normal has positive $z$-component and $n_z\,dS=dxdy$; on the lower surface $z=z_1$ the outward normal has negative $z$-component and $n_z\,dS=-dxdy$; the lateral surface has normal perpendicular to the $z$-axis, so $n_z=0$. Hence $$\oiint_\Sigma R n_z\,dS=\iint_D R(x,y,z_2)\,dxdy-\iint_D R(x,y,z_1)\,dxdy.$$ The two expressions agree, i.e. $\oiint_\Sigma R n_z\,dS=\iiint_\Omega R_z\,dV$.

For the $P$-component, if $\Omega$ is $x$-simple (each line parallel to the $x$-axis enters and leaves once), the fundamental theorem of calculus similarly gives $$\oiint_\Sigma P n_x\,dS=\iiint_\Omega P_x\,dV;$$ for $Q$, regarding $\Omega$ as $y$-simple gives $$\oiint_\Sigma Q n_y\,dS=\iiint_\Omega Q_y\,dV.$$ Adding the three identities, the left side is $\oiint_\Sigma(P n_x+Q n_y+R n_z)\,dS=\oiint_\Sigma F\cdot n\,dS$ and the right side is $\iiint_\Omega(P_x+Q_y+R_z)\,dV$, which is Gauss's theorem. If $\Omega$ cannot be written as all three simple types at once, cut it by finitely many piecewise smooth surfaces into finitely many such subregions; on each internal cut surface the outward normals of the two sides are opposite, so the fluxes cancel, and the triple integral is additive, so the conclusion persists.

Orientation check: let $\Omega$ be the unit ball $x^2+y^2+z^2\le1$ and $F=(x,y,z)$. Then $\operatorname{div}F=3$, so $$\oiint_\Sigma F\cdot n\,dS=\iiint_\Omega3\,dV=3\cdot\frac{4\pi}{3}=4\pi.$$ Directly: the outward unit normal on the sphere is $n=(x,y,z)$, and on the sphere $F\cdot n=x^2+y^2+z^2=1$, so the flux is $\oiint_\Sigma1\,dS=4\pi$, in agreement. If the inner side were used by mistake, $n$ would become $-(x,y,z)$ and the flux $-4\pi$; this shows that the 'outer normal' is not a harmless convention.

Shrink $\Omega$ to an interior point $M$. If $F$ is $C^1$ at $M$, then $\operatorname{div}F$ is continuous at $M$; by the mean value theorem for integrals (or the intermediate value property) there is $M_\Omega\in\Omega$ such that $$\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{V(\Omega)}&\oiint_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot n\,dS\\&=\frac{1}{V(\Omega)}\iiint_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dV=\operatorname{div}F(M_\Omega).\end{aligned}$$ As $\Omega$ shrinks to $M$, $M_\Omega\to M$, and continuity gives $$\operatorname{div}F(M)=\lim_{\Omega\to M}\frac{1}{V(\Omega)}\oiint_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot n\,dS.$$ This is the precise meaning of 'divergence is flux per unit volume': positive divergence indicates a source, negative divergence a sink. The limit requires the regions to shrink in a controlled way and $F$ to be $C^1$ in a neighborhood of $M$.

Gauss's theorem requires $F$ to be $C^1$ everywhere on $\Omega$; singularities cannot be ignored. For example $F(r)=r/|r|^3$ ($r\ne0$) satisfies $\operatorname{div}F=0$, but for $\Sigma$ the sphere of radius $\varepsilon$ centred at the origin, taken outward, a direct computation on the sphere gives $n=r/\varepsilon$, $F\cdot n=1/\varepsilon^2$, hence $$\oiint_\Sigma F\cdot n\,dS=\frac{1}{\varepsilon^2}\cdot4\pi\varepsilon^2=4\pi\ne0.$$ If Gauss's theorem is applied to the region $\{\varepsilon\le|r|\le1\}$, the divergence inside is $0$, while the outer sphere contributes $4\pi$ and the inner sphere contributes $-4\pi$ (the outward normal of that region points toward the origin on the inner sphere), totaling $0$, consistent with the triple integral. Thus, when a singularity lies inside the region, $\Sigma$ cannot simply be shrunk to a point; one must excavate a small ball and apply the theorem to the punctured region.

zh: 设 $\Sigma$ 是分片光滑的有向曲面，单位法向量 $n$ 选定一侧；其边界 $\Gamma=\partial\Sigma$ 是分段光滑闭曲线，取向与 $n$ 成右手法则：右手四指沿 $\Gamma$ 弯曲时，拇指指向 $n$。设 $F=(P,Q,R)$ 在包含 $\Sigma$ 的区域上有连续一阶偏导数。则 $$\oint_\Gamma F\cdot dr=\iint_\Sigma(\nabla\times F)\cdot n\,dS.$$ 坐标形式为 $$\begin{aligned}\oint_\Gamma &P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz\\&=\iint_\Sigma(R_y-Q_z)\,dy\,dz+(P_z-R_x)\,dz\,dx\\&\qquad+(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\,dy.\end{aligned}$$ 条件：$\Gamma$ 是 $\Sigma$ 的边界、定向与 $n$ 右手匹配、$F$ 在 $\Sigma$ 附近 $C^1$。

先设 $\Sigma$ 是图 $z=f(x,y)$，$(x,y)\in D$，$f$ 有连续二阶偏导数，取上侧。参数化 $r(x,y)=(x,y,f(x,y))$，则 $$n\,dS=(-f_x,-f_y,1)\,dx\,dy.$$ $\Gamma$ 的定向由右手法则诱导，在边界投影为一对一的标准情形下，它投影为 $D$ 的正向边界。沿 $\Gamma$ 有 $dz=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy$，故 $$\begin{aligned}\oint_\Gamma P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz&=\oint_{\partial D}(P+Rf_x)\,dx\\&\qquad+(Q+Rf_y)\,dy.\end{aligned}$$ 对右端用格林公式：$$\iint_D\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(Q+Rf_y)-\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(P+Rf_x)\right]dxdy.$$ 展开时含 $f_{xy}$ 的项相消，得 $$\iint_D\left[(Q_x-P_y)+(Q_z-R_y)f_x+(R_x-P_z)f_y\right]dxdy.$$ 而 $$(\nabla\times F)\cdot n\,dS=\left[-(R_y-Q_z)f_x-(P_z-R_x)f_y+(Q_x-P_y)\right]dxdy,$$ 两者相同，故公式对图形成立。

对一般分片光滑曲面，用有限个参数片把它分成有限块，每块或是图 $z=f(x,y)$，或是图 $x=g(y,z)$、$y=h(z,x)$；在每种情形下同上把 $F$ 拉回到参数平面、用格林公式，得到该片上的斯托克斯公式。把所有片相加：相邻两片的公共边界在两张片上诱导的方向相反，线积分沿公共边相消，只剩外边界 $\Gamma$；曲面积分对分片可加。因此公式对分片光滑的有向曲面成立。$\Sigma$ 允许有边界角点，只要 $\Gamma$ 分段光滑、各参数片足够正则。

定向必须成对出现。若把 $\Sigma$ 的法向改为 $-n$，为保持右手法则，$\Gamma$ 也必须反向，于是等式两端同时变号，公式仍成立；若只改 $\Sigma$ 的定向而保持 $\Gamma$ 不变，右端变号而左端不变，等式一般不再成立。平面特例：取 $\Sigma$ 为 $xy$ 平面内区域 $D$、$n=k$，右手法则给出的 $\Gamma$ 正是 $D$ 的逆时针正向，此时 $(\nabla\times F)\cdot n=Q_x-P_y$，斯托克斯公式退化为格林公式。若取 $n=-k$，则 $\Gamma$ 应取顺时针，两端同时变号。

设 $\Sigma_1,\Sigma_2$ 是以同一条有向闭曲线 $\Gamma$ 为边界的两张分片光滑曲面，且它们一起围成区域 $V$（或可分割成若干这样的区域）。给 $\Sigma_2$ 取相反定向 $-\Sigma_2$，则 $\Sigma_1\cup(-\Sigma_2)$ 是 $V$ 的外向闭曲面。若 $F$ 在 $V$ 上 $C^2$，则 $\operatorname{div}(
abla	imes F)=0$，由高斯公式 $$\oiint_{\Sigma_1\cup(-\Sigma_2)}(
abla	imes F)\cdot n\,dS=\iiint_V\operatorname{div}(
abla	imes F)\,dV=0.$$ 故 $$\iint_{\Sigma_1}(
abla	imes F)\cdot n\,dS=\iint_{\Sigma_2}(
abla	imes F)\cdot n\,dS.$$ 这就是斯托克斯公式的「曲面可替换性」：只要边界与定向相同，选哪张曲面都可以，常用来把难算曲面换成平面圆盘。条件 $F\in C^2$ 用于保证经典等式 $\operatorname{div}\operatorname{curl}F=0$ 成立。

例：$F=(-y,x,0)$，$\Gamma$ 为 $xy$ 平面内单位圆，逆时针。取 $\Sigma$ 为圆盘 $x^2+y^2\le1,\ z=0$，$n=k$。则 $\nabla\times F=(0,0,2)$，$$\iint_\Sigma(\nabla\times F)\cdot n\,dS=\iint_\Sigma2\,dxdy=2\pi.$$ 直接算线积分：$x=\cos t,\ y=\sin t,\ t:0\to2\pi$，$$\oint_\Gamma -y\,dx+x\,dy=\int_0^{2\pi}(\sin^2t+\cos^2t)\,dt=2\pi.$$ 两者一致。若把 $\Gamma$ 改成顺时针而仍取 $n=k$，线积分为 $-2\pi$，与右手法则不符；此时应同时把 $n$ 改为 $-k$，右端也变为 $-2\pi$。另需注意 $F$ 必须在 $\Sigma$ 的邻域内 $C^1$，曲面穿过奇点时必须先挖去。
en: Let $\Sigma$ be a piecewise smooth oriented surface with a chosen unit normal $n$, and let its boundary $\Gamma=\partial\Sigma$ be a piecewise smooth closed curve oriented by the right-hand rule: when the fingers of the right hand curl along $\Gamma$, the thumb points along $n$. Let $F=(P,Q,R)$ have continuous first partial derivatives on a region containing $\Sigma$. Then $$\oint_\Gamma F\cdot dr=\iint_\Sigma(\nabla\times F)\cdot n\,dS.$$ In coordinates, $$\begin{aligned}\oint_\Gamma &P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz\\&=\iint_\Sigma(R_y-Q_z)\,dy\,dz+(P_z-R_x)\,dz\,dx\\&\qquad+(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\,dy.\end{aligned}$$ Hypotheses: $\Gamma$ is the boundary of $\Sigma$, its orientation matches $n$ by the right-hand rule, and $F$ is $C^1$ near $\Sigma$.

First suppose $\Sigma$ is the graph $z=f(x,y)$ over $(x,y)\in D$, with $f$ of class $C^2$, taken with the upward normal. Parametrize $r(x,y)=(x,y,f(x,y))$; then $$n\,dS=(-f_x,-f_y,1)\,dx\,dy.$$ The orientation of $\Gamma$ induced by the right-hand rule projects to the positive boundary of $D$ (in the standard case where the projection is one-to-one). Along $\Gamma$, $dz=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy$, so $$\begin{aligned}\oint_\Gamma P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz&=\oint_{\partial D}(P+Rf_x)\,dx\\&\qquad+(Q+Rf_y)\,dy.\end{aligned}$$ Applying Green's theorem to the right side gives $$\iint_D\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(Q+Rf_y)-\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(P+Rf_x)\right]dxdy.$$ In the expansion the terms containing $f_{xy}$ cancel, leaving $$\iint_D\left[(Q_x-P_y)+(Q_z-R_y)f_x+(R_x-P_z)f_y\right]dxdy.$$ On the other hand, $$(\nabla\times F)\cdot n\,dS=\left[-(R_y-Q_z)f_x-(P_z-R_x)f_y+(Q_x-P_y)\right]dxdy,$$ which is the same. Hence the formula holds for graphs.

For a general piecewise smooth surface, cut it by finitely many parameter patches into finitely many pieces, each of which is a graph $z=f(x,y)$, $x=g(y,z)$, or $y=h(z,x)$; in each case pull $F$ back to the parameter plane and apply Green's theorem as above to obtain Stokes' theorem on that patch. Summing over all patches: on a common edge of two adjacent patches the induced orientations are opposite, so the line integrals cancel and only the outer boundary $\Gamma$ remains; the surface integral is additive over patches. Hence the formula holds for piecewise smooth oriented surfaces. Corners on $\Sigma$ are allowed as long as $\Gamma$ is piecewise smooth and the parameter patches are regular enough.

Orientations must be paired. If the normal of $\Sigma$ is changed to $-n$, then to preserve the right-hand rule $\Gamma$ must also be reversed; both sides change sign and the identity still holds. If only $\Sigma$ is reoriented while $\Gamma$ is kept, the right side changes sign and the left does not, so the identity generally fails. Plane special case: take $\Sigma$ to be a region $D$ in the $xy$-plane with $n=k$; the right-hand rule gives $\Gamma$ the counterclockwise positive orientation, and $(\nabla\times F)\cdot n=Q_x-P_y$, so Stokes' theorem reduces to Green's theorem. With $n=-k$, $\Gamma$ must be clockwise and both sides change sign.

Let $\Sigma_1,\Sigma_2$ be two piecewise smooth surfaces with the same oriented boundary $\Gamma$ that together bound a region $V$ (or can be split into finitely many such regions). Give $\Sigma_2$ the opposite orientation $-\Sigma_2$; then $\Sigma_1\cup(-\Sigma_2)$ is the outward closed surface of $V$. If $F$ is $C^2$ on $V$, then $\operatorname{div}(
abla	imes F)=0$, and Gauss's theorem gives $$\oiint_{\Sigma_1\cup(-\Sigma_2)}(
abla	imes F)\cdot n\,dS=\iiint_V\operatorname{div}(
abla	imes F)\,dV=0.$$ Hence $$\iint_{\Sigma_1}(
abla	imes F)\cdot n\,dS=\iint_{\Sigma_2}(
abla	imes F)\cdot n\,dS.$$ This is the 'surface-independence' of Stokes' theorem: as long as the boundary and orientation are the same, any surface may be used, which is often exploited to replace a complicated surface by a flat disk. The hypothesis $F\in C^2$ ensures the classical identity $\operatorname{div}\operatorname{curl}F=0$.

Example: $F=(-y,x,0)$, $\Gamma$ the unit circle in the $xy$-plane, counterclockwise. Take $\Sigma$ to be the disk $x^2+y^2\le1,\ z=0$ with $n=k$. Then $\nabla\times F=(0,0,2)$, so $$\iint_\Sigma(\nabla\times F)\cdot n\,dS=\iint_\Sigma2\,dxdy=2\pi.$$ Directly, with $x=\cos t,\ y=\sin t,\ t:0\to2\pi$, $$\oint_\Gamma -y\,dx+x\,dy=\int_0^{2\pi}(\sin^2t+\cos^2t)\,dt=2\pi.$$ The two agree. If $\Gamma$ is made clockwise while $n=k$ is kept, the line integral is $-2\pi$, which violates the right-hand rule; one should simultaneously change $n$ to $-k$, and the right side also becomes $-2\pi$. Note also that $F$ must be $C^1$ in a neighborhood of $\Sigma$; if the surface passes through a singularity, it must first be punctured.

zh: 设 $T:D'\to D$，$(u,v)\mapsto(x(u,v),y(u,v))$，$x,y$ 有连续偏导数。$T$ 在点 $(u,v)$ 的微分是线性映射 $$\begin{aligned}DT&=\begin{pmatrix}x_u&x_v\\ y_u&y_v\end{pmatrix},\\ T(u+h,v+k)&=T(u,v)+DT\binom{h}{k}+o\left(\sqrt{h^2+k^2}\right).\end{aligned}$$ 其行列式 $$J=\det DT=\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=x_uy_v-x_vy_u$$ 称为雅可比行列式。它一般是 $(u,v)$ 的函数，刻画 $T$ 在一点附近的线性主部。

看 $uv$ 平面上以 $(u,v)$ 为顶点、边长为 $h,k$ 的小矩形。两条边向量 $(h,0),(0,k)$ 被 $DT$ 映成 $$h(x_u,y_u),\qquad k(x_v,y_v).$$ 这两个向量张成的平行四边形面积等于它们构成的 $2\times2$ 行列式的绝对值：$$\left|\det\begin{pmatrix}hx_u&kx_v\\ hy_u&ky_v\end{pmatrix}\right|=|hk(x_uy_v-x_vy_u)|=|J|\,hk.$$ 因此 $|J|$ 是局部面积伸缩率；$J$ 的符号表示定向：$J>0$ 保持定向，$J<0$ 翻转定向（如交换两个坐标轴）。

把 $D'$ 分成小矩形网格，第 $i$ 块面积为 $\Delta u_i\Delta v_i$，在内部取点 $(u_i,v_i)$。其像块面积近似为 $|J(u_i,v_i)|\Delta u_i\Delta v_i$，且当网格直径趋于零时相对误差一致地趋于零（$T$ 在紧集上 $C^1$）。对 $D$ 上的连续函数 $f$，以像块为分割、以 $T(u_i,v_i)$ 为取样点作黎曼和：$$\sum_i f(T(u_i,v_i))\,|J(u_i,v_i)|\Delta u_i\Delta v_i.$$ 它正是 $\iint_{D'}f(T(u,v))|J(u,v)|\,dudv$ 的黎曼和；另一方面它趋于 $\iint_D f(x,y)\,dxdy$。故 $$\iint_D f\,dxdy=\iint_{D'}f(T(u,v))\,|J|\,dudv.$$ 这要求 $T$ 在内部一一对应、$J\ne0$（至多除零面积集）、$f$ 连续（或可积）。

为什么必须加绝对值？微分形式意义下 $dx\wedge dy=J\,du\wedge dv$，这里 $J$ 可正可负；但重积分用的是无向面积测度，面积元素恒非负。若 $J<0$，映射翻转定向，$dx\wedge dy$ 与 $du\wedge dv$ 的定向相反，两个定向面积元相差一个负号；取绝对值后伸缩因子仍是 $|J|$。例：$x=v,\ y=u$，$J=-1$，但 $$\iint_D f(x,y)\,dxdy=\iint_{D'}f(v,u)\,dudv,$$ 面积不变；若写成 $J\,dudv$ 会得到负值。一维情形同理：$$\int f(x)\,dx=\int f(\varphi(t))|\varphi'(t)|\,dt,$$ 当 $\varphi$ 递减时不能丢掉绝对值。注意曲线积分 $\int P\,dx+Q\,dy$ 是有向积分，换元时不取绝对值，这与二重积分、三重积分不同。

三重情形完全平行：若 $T:(u,v,w)\mapsto(x,y,z)$ 是 $C^1$、内部一一对应，且雅可比 $$J=\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}=\begin{vmatrix}x_u&x_v&x_w\\ y_u&y_v&y_w\\ z_u&z_v&z_w\end{vmatrix}$$ 除零体积集外非零，则 $$\iiint_\Omega f\,dV=\iiint_{\Omega'}f(T(u,v,w))\,|J|\,du\,dv\,dw.$$ 两个标准特例：柱坐标 $x=r\cos\theta,\ y=r\sin\theta,\ z=z$ 给出 $J=r$，$dV=r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz$；球坐标 $x=\rho\sin\varphi\cos\theta,\ y=\rho\sin\varphi\sin\theta,\ z=\rho\cos\varphi$ 给出 $J=\rho^2\sin\varphi$，在 $0\le\varphi\le\pi$ 上 $|J|=\rho^2\sin\varphi$，故 $dV=\rho^2\sin\varphi\,d\rho\,d\varphi\,d\theta$。

使用换元公式前要核对三件事：（1）$T$ 在区域内部一一对应，否则同一像点被重复计算；（2）$J\ne0$ 除零测集外，否则 $T$ 把区域压到低维，如 $(u,v)\mapsto(u,0)$ 的 $J\equiv0$，像面积为 $0$ 而 $\iint dudv$ 不为零，公式失效；（3）$f$ 在 $D$ 上可积。$J\ne0$ 的点由反函数定理保证 $T$ 有局部 $C^1$ 逆，这是换元公式局部成立的依据；$J=0$ 只允许出现在零面积或零体积的集合上（如极坐标的 $r=0$、球坐标的 $\rho=0$ 或 $\varphi=0,\pi$）。最后再提醒：二重积分、三重积分取 $|J|$，有向曲线积分与微分形式换元不取绝对值。
en: Let $T:D'\to D$, $(u,v)\mapsto(x(u,v),y(u,v))$, with $x,y$ continuously differentiable. The differential of $T$ at $(u,v)$ is the linear map $$\begin{aligned}DT&=\begin{pmatrix}x_u&x_v\\ y_u&y_v\end{pmatrix},\\ T(u+h,v+k)&=T(u,v)+DT\binom{h}{k}+o\left(\sqrt{h^2+k^2}\right).\end{aligned}$$ Its determinant $$J=\det DT=\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=x_uy_v-x_vy_u$$ is the Jacobian determinant. It is generally a function of $(u,v)$ and describes the linear principal part of $T$ near a point.

Consider a small rectangle in the $uv$-plane with vertex $(u,v)$ and side lengths $h,k$. The edge vectors $(h,0),(0,k)$ are mapped by $DT$ to $$h(x_u,y_u),\qquad k(x_v,y_v).$$ The area of the parallelogram spanned by these vectors is the absolute value of their $2\times2$ determinant: $$\left|\det\begin{pmatrix}hx_u&kx_v\\ hy_u&ky_v\end{pmatrix}\right|=|hk(x_uy_v-x_vy_u)|=|J|\,hk.$$ Hence $|J|$ is the local area scaling factor; the sign of $J$ records orientation: $J>0$ preserves it, $J<0$ reverses it (e.g. swapping the two coordinate axes).

Partition $D'$ into a rectangular grid with $i$-th cell area $\Delta u_i\Delta v_i$ and choose $(u_i,v_i)$ inside it. The image cell has area approximately $|J(u_i,v_i)|\Delta u_i\Delta v_i$, and the relative error tends uniformly to zero as the mesh tends to zero ($T$ is $C^1$ on a compact set). For a continuous $f$ on $D$, use the image cells as a partition and $T(u_i,v_i)$ as sample points: $$\sum_i f(T(u_i,v_i))\,|J(u_i,v_i)|\Delta u_i\Delta v_i.$$ This is a Riemann sum for $\iint_{D'}f(T(u,v))|J(u,v)|\,dudv$; on the other hand it tends to $\iint_D f(x,y)\,dxdy$. Hence $$\iint_D f\,dxdy=\iint_{D'}f(T(u,v))\,|J|\,dudv.$$ This requires $T$ one-to-one on the interior, $J\ne0$ except on a null set, and $f$ continuous (or integrable).

Why the absolute value? In the language of differential forms $dx\wedge dy=J\,du\wedge dv$, where $J$ may be positive or negative; but multiple integrals use the unoriented area measure, which is nonnegative. If $J<0$ the map reverses orientation, so $dx\wedge dy$ and $du\wedge dv$ have opposite orientations and the two oriented area elements differ by a sign; after taking absolute values the scaling factor is still $|J|$. Example: $x=v,\ y=u$ has $J=-1$, yet $$\iint_D f(x,y)\,dxdy=\iint_{D'}f(v,u)\,dudv,$$ so the area is unchanged; writing $J\,dudv$ would give a negative value. The one-dimensional case is the same: $$\int f(x)\,dx=\int f(\varphi(t))|\varphi'(t)|\,dt,$$ and the absolute value cannot be dropped when $\varphi$ is decreasing. Note that a line integral $\int P\,dx+Q\,dy$ is oriented; under substitution it does not take an absolute value, unlike double and triple integrals.

The triple case is completely parallel: if $T:(u,v,w)\mapsto(x,y,z)$ is $C^1$, one-to-one on the interior, and its Jacobian $$J=\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}=\begin{vmatrix}x_u&x_v&x_w\\ y_u&y_v&y_w\\ z_u&z_v&z_w\end{vmatrix}$$ is nonzero off a set of volume zero, then $$\iiint_\Omega f\,dV=\iiint_{\Omega'}f(T(u,v,w))\,|J|\,du\,dv\,dw.$$ Two standard special cases: cylindrical coordinates $x=r\cos\theta,\ y=r\sin\theta,\ z=z$ give $J=r$ and $dV=r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz$; spherical coordinates $x=\rho\sin\varphi\cos\theta,\ y=\rho\sin\varphi\sin\theta,\ z=\rho\cos\varphi$ give $J=\rho^2\sin\varphi$, and since $\sin\varphi\ge0$ on $0\le\varphi\le\pi$, $|J|=\rho^2\sin\varphi$, hence $dV=\rho^2\sin\varphi\,d\rho\,d\varphi\,d\theta$.

Before using the change-of-variables formula, check three things: (1) $T$ is one-to-one on the interior, otherwise the same image point is counted twice; (2) $J
e0$ off a null set, otherwise $T$ collapses the region to lower dimension — for $(u,v)\mapsto(u,0)$, $J\equiv0$, the image has area $0$ while $\iint dudv
e0$, so the formula fails; (3) $f$ is integrable on $D$. At points where $J
e0$, the inverse function theorem guarantees a local $C^1$ inverse, which is the basis for the local validity of the formula; $J=0$ is allowed only on sets of zero area or volume (such as $r=0$ in polar coordinates, or $ho=0$ and $\varphi=0,\pi$ in spherical coordinates). Finally, double and triple integrals take $|J|$, whereas oriented line integrals and differential-form substitutions do not.
